samples.summary: revokeInvite resolves the workspace id a third time, duplicating work the layer above and assertOwner already did. The controller (workspace.controller.ts:109) calls `resolveId(idOrSlug)` before invoking the service, and `assertOwner` (line 216) itself calls `resolveId` again. The new `const resolvedId = await this.resolveId(workspaceId)` is therefore a third identical lookup. The existing pieces can be reused instead: `assertOwner` already returns the `WorkspaceMember` row, so `member.workspaceId` (or having assertOwner return the resolved id) gives the scoped id with no extra query. The scoping fix itself is the right call; only the way it obtains the id duplicates existing resolution logic.

The delta introduces two contradictory contracts for the `workspaceId` parameter within the same service. `createInvite` (line 116) and `findInvites` (line 128) use the incoming `workspaceId` verbatim in Prisma `where`/`data`, i.e. they assume the caller already passed a resolved UUID (which the controller guarantees). `revokeInvite` now assumes the opposite and re-resolves. Whichever convention is intended, it should be uniform across the invite methods; as written a future caller reading revokeInvite will reasonably assume slugs are accepted service-wide and silently get empty results from findInvites / an FK error from createInvite.

revokeInvite's return shape changed from the deleted Prisma `WorkspaceInvite` record to `{ id: inviteId }`, a narrowing of the DELETE /workspaces/:id/invites/:inviteId response body. No consumer in the tree reads it (packages/frontend/src/api/workspaces.ts:138 returns `Promise<void>`), so this is safe today, but it is an undocumented API-surface change riding along with a scoping fix; worth stating deliberately (e.g. return 204 / no body) rather than leaving a half-shaped object.
